tagline.text: A Korean-style pilgrimage site in Lolomboy, Bulacan, tied to Father Andrew Kim

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Lolomboy, Bocaue, Bulacan, at the Parish of Nuestro Señor Jesucristo

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (around the September 20 feast of the Korean martyrs is also meaningful)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,200 (round trip by public transport from Manila plus a donation, per person)

children.text: The Shrine of Saint Andrew Kim is a diocesan shrine in Lolomboy, Bocaue, Bulacan, where Korea's first priest, Father Andrew Kim Taegon, is said to have stayed and studied for the priesthood in the 1830s and 1840s. With its Korean-style pagoda, meditation room and pilgrims' museum, it is a quiet place to meet the roots of Korean Catholicism in the Philippines.

The official name is the Parish of Nuestro Señor Jesucristo and Diocesan Shrine of Saint Andrew Kim Taegon. It stands in Barangay Lolomboy in the town of Bocaue, Bulacan, north of Manila, and belongs to the Diocese of Malolos. It lies roughly
30km
north of central Manila, and public transport takes about
1.5–2 hours
depending on traffic.

The shrine matters to Koreans because of Father Andrew Kim. Andrew Kim Taegon was the first Korean-born Catholic priest and a martyr saint. Chosen by priests of the Paris Foreign Missions Society, he studied at the seminary in Macau, and in the 1830s and 1840s he is said to have continued his studies at the Dominican hacienda in Lolomboy (the Hacienda de Lolomboy) to escape unrest in China. Some sources record that he stayed in 1837, 1839 and 1841 and served as an interpreter for Dominican missionaries. Because of this link, the parish made him its secondary patron after his canonization in 1984.

The shrine looks quite different from other Philippine churches. A building with white walls and black accents mixes hanok, Eastern and Renaissance elements, and the grounds include a seven-story pagoda, a pyramid-shaped meditation room built of stone, a small chapel with frescoes, a lake and a bamboo garden. News reports describe an older shrine built in Korean style with a pilgrims' museum and a 15-tier pagoda. The Sisters of St. Andrew, a Korean congregation, live on site and care for the shrine.

Keep in mind that this is a place for prayer and rest, not a showy tourist attraction. There is no admission fee, but silence and modest dress are expected, and since opening hours and visiting rules change often, it is safest to check with the parish before you go. It makes an easy pilgrimage day trip for Korean worshippers visiting the Philippines and for Korean families living here. This is not a paid attraction for Korean tourists but a living church run by the local parish. Groups visiting as a pilgrimage should contact the parish or the sisters in advance to arrange visiting times and guidance.

Father Andrew Kim is said to have taken refuge at the Dominican hacienda in Lolomboy and studied there during his years at the Macau seminary. He was canonized in Seoul on May 6, 1984, among the 103 Korean martyr saints, and the parish honors him as a secondary patron. It is a rare point of contact between Korean Catholic history and the Philippines. Visitors can follow his journey through the information boards and the statue of the saint. Ask on site whether Korean-language guidance is available.

blocks.title: A church that blends hanok and Western styles

children.text: The main building, with white walls and black accents, is described as a blend of Renaissance, Eastern and hanok elements. It is an unusual sight: roof lines that look like a Korean drama set in the middle of the Philippines. Construction of the new church began in 2001 and was completed in 2015. Walk around the outside to look at the roof lines, tiles and window shapes.

The small chapel beside the main building has murals of Korean martyrs, angels and apostles, along with paintings inspired by the Sistine Chapel. It is small but calm, and a good place to sit for a while. Follow the instructions on site for lighting candles.

The stone, pyramid-shaped meditation room is topped with a roof of hanok-style tiles. Visitor accounts say the inside is air-conditioned, so it is a good place to cool off and pray on a hot day. Please stay quiet inside.

The shrine's seven-story pagoda is described as symbolizing the seven sacraments of the Catholic Church. It resembles a Korean temple pagoda but its meaning belongs to the church, so remember that this is a religious site when you take photos. News reports also mention a 15-tier pagoda at the older shrine, so check the information boards on site.

It was reported that at the Mass declaring the diocesan shrine on January 30, 2021, a pilgrims' museum was blessed in the old shrine in Lolomboy. The museum is run by the parish and the Sisters of St. Andrew and introduces Father Andrew Kim's journey and the Korean martyrs. Opening hours may not be fixed. Exhibits may change, so confirm with the parish before you visit.

One side of the shrine has a garden with a view of a lake and a river, planted with bamboo and fruit trees. Another story says the altar cross was made from the wood of a mango tree that comforted the homesick seminarian. The walking paths are short, so it is an easy stroll.

On May 2, 1986, the parish became a spiritual twin of the Saenamteo martyrs' shrine and parish in Seoul. It is said that Stephen Cardinal Kim, then Archbishop of Seoul, gave the parish a statue of the saint that same year. It is a point to look for as a trace of the exchange with Korea.

items.title: Half-day pilgrimage course
items.subtitle: Lolomboy shrine and a look around Bocaue

children.text: Take a bus bound for Bocaue from EDSA Cubao or a similar stop in Manila. Leaving around
helps you avoid the midday heat and the evening rush.
Get off near the Bocaue NLEX exit, transfer to a jeepney bound for Monumento, Meycauayan or Marilao, and get off in front of McDonald's Lolomboy.
Take a tricycle or walk from McDonald's to the shrine. First say a short prayer in the main church and the candle chapel.
Take your time around the pyramid-shaped meditation room, the seven-story pagoda and the garden by the lake. Check the guidance before taking photos.
If it is open, see the pilgrims' museum and buy a cross or rosary at the souvenir shop.
Have lunch in Lolomboy or Bocaue town and head back.
Opening hours are sometimes split around a midday break, so avoid arriving around noon and aim to get there in the morning.

items.title: Full-day itinerary
items.subtitle: A route linking the shrine and Bulacan's historic towns

children.text: Drive to the Bocaue NLEX exit and then on to the Lolomboy shrine.
After your visit, stay quietly to pray or check the Mass schedule.
Have lunch in town.
See the area around Meycauayan Church or head toward the Obando shrine.
Leave for Manila before traffic gets heavy.

Visitors report that the street in front of the shrine is narrow with little parking, so avoid large vehicles or park farther away.
Fly from Incheon to Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) in Manila.
From the airport to Bocaue can take
1.5–2.5 hours
or more depending on traffic, so leave plenty of room in your day.
The shrine involves walking and moving outdoors, so the dry season with less rain is more comfortable. November to May is relatively stable, but March to May is very hot.
Korean Catholics may want to time a visit around September 20, the feast of the Korean martyrs. Events can vary from year to year, so check the parish announcements.

items.note: Donations and souvenir purchases are the custom

The shrine is a quiet space run by a convent, so most people visit for the day rather than stay overnight. A retreat house is mentioned, but whether outside guests can stay there and at what price must be asked of the parish directly.
For meals, use the restaurants around McDonald's Lolomboy and along the national highway through Bocaue and Marilao. If you want Korean food, it is better to plan lunch in Manila beforehand.

Before heading back to Manila from Lolomboy, you can try Filipino home cooking at a restaurant along the Bocaue highway. Rather than a specific place, a busy one is a safe choice, and if you need Korean food, bring it from Manila's Korean neighborhood in advance.
There is no admission fee, but it is good manners to put a small donation in the box or buy something from the souvenir shop.
The shrine is a quiet space run by a convent. Do not talk loudly or take phone calls.
Avoid shorts and sleeveless tops and dress modestly.
Opening hours differ by source (7 AM–5 PM, 8 AM–5 PM, partial morning and afternoon opening and so on). It may be closed on Mondays, so check with the parish before you visit.
English Masses are said to be held on the second and fourth Saturdays of each month, so plan your visit accordingly if you want to attend.
The streets are narrow if you drive, so use a small car or take public transport.
Arrive in the morning to avoid the hottest hours, and bring water and an umbrella.
Reading a little about Father Andrew Kim's life in advance will make the exhibits and murals more meaningful.
This is a religious site, so follow the rules on photography and silence, and be sure to confirm opening hours and visiting rules with the parish.
Opening hours and closing days differ by source, so you may make the trip for nothing.
The road in front of the shrine is narrow and parking is hard.
Roads can flood in the rainy season, so check the weather.
NLEX and MacArthur Highway are very congested at rush hour.
Ask permission before photographing the sisters and worshippers.
Obando, about
30 minutes
by car, has a church famous for a festival in which people pray for fertility. You can visit it on the same day.
A city to the south of Lolomboy where you can see an old church and living heritage. It is easy to combine into a day trip along the same highway.
The center of the Diocese of Malolos, to which the shrine belongs, where you can also see sites of Philippine independence history. Travel time varies greatly with traffic, so leave some margin.

In Bocaue, a pagoda festival famous for its boat procession on the river is held around the first Sunday of July. It is in the same town as the shrine, so time your visit to it if you like, but expect very large crowds.
